title: Bede: the sparrow in the hall (Ecclesiastical History II.13)
passage_first_words: The present life of man upon earth, O king, seems to me, in comparison with that time which is unknown to us, like to the swift flight of a sparrow through the house wherein you sit at supper in winter
where_found: eoforwic (the minster school's copy; the speech was made near York in 627); also gyrwe, where Bede wrote it, until the raid of 794; any English minster with act:read_text
translator: A. M. Sellar (death year not found (?)); fallback J. A. Giles (d. 1884), Bohn 1847
why: The best-known image in the period's best-known history, and a heathen counsellor's own words about not knowing what comes after: it suits a crew of two faiths. First words checked against Gutenberg #38326.

title: Bede: Caedmon the cowherd is told to sing (Ecclesiastical History IV.24)
passage_first_words: For having lived in the secular habit till he was well advanced in years, he had never learned anything of versifying; and for this reason sometimes at a banquet, when it was agreed to make merry by singing in turn, if he saw the harp come towards him, he would rise up from table and go out and return home.
where_found: streonaeshalch (Whitby, where it happened, c. 670); eoforwic
translator: A. M. Sellar (death year not found (?)); fallback J. A. Giles (d. 1884), Bohn 1847
why: Shows how song went by mouth: the harp passed round the table and every man sang in turn. A card for a feast (act:song) can use it. Checked against Gutenberg #38326.

title: Bede: the books of Wearmouth and Jarrow (Lives of the Abbots, 11 and 15)
passage_first_words: The large and noble library, which he had brought from Rome, and which was necessary for the edification of his church, he commanded to be kept entire, and neither by neglect to be injured or dispersed.
where_found: gyrwe (Jarrow) until 794; afterwards a copy at eoforwic
why: Gives the only firm book price of the age: one volume of the Geographers bought at Rome was traded to King Aldfrith for eight hides of land; and the three great Bibles (pandects), one of which went to Rome. The Fordham page prints Giles from the Everyman reprint of 1910; first printed 1843-45 (the exact first year unchecked (?)). Take the shipped text from a printed scan, not from Fordham's page (its electronic form is marked not for commercial use).

title: Adamnan: Columba stops at the foot of the page (Life of Columba III.23)
passage_first_words: After these words he descended the hill, and having returned to the monastery sat in his hut transcribing the Psalter, and coming to that verse of the 33d Psalm
where_found: hi (Iona) until the community moves most of its treasures to Kells from 807; duiblinn's hinterland churches later (?)
why: A saint dies as a scribe: 'Here, at the end of the page, I must stop; and what follows let Baithene write.' The right text to be shown at Iona's writing hut. Checked against the Fordham copy of Reeves 1874; ship from the 1874 scan.

title: Boniface asks Abbess Eadburg for the Epistles of Peter in letters of gold (735)
passage_first_words: So now I beg thee to carry still further what thou hast begun, and to copy in gold the Epistles of my lord, Saint Peter, that the Holy Scriptures may be honoured and reverenced when the preacher holds them before the eyes of the heathen
where_found: mogontia (Mainz kept Boniface's letter book under Lul and after); traiectum (Utrecht, his first mission); sarre and fordwic stand nearest to Thanet, where Eadburg's women wrote it
why: A book made to be seen by people who cannot read it, a woman's scriptorium, and a letter carried over the sea by a named priest (Eoba). It is the seed of a carrying job: gold leaf out, a book back. Checked against the scan's text (the scan's misprint 'my be honoured' corrected to 'may').

title: Charlemagne to Abbot Baugulf of Fulda, on the study of letters (De litteris colendis)
passage_first_words: Be it known, therefore, to your devotion pleasing to God, that we, together with our faithful, have considered it to be useful that the bishoprics and monasteries entrusted by the favor of Christ to our control
where_found: mogontia (the nearest port to Fulda: the letter was to be copied to every bishop and monastery); colonia; parisius (Saint-Denis)
why: The king's own complaint that the monks' letters to him had 'correct thoughts and uncouth expressions'. It explains why every abbey on the Rhine is hungry for good exemplars in 793. Date c. 780-800. Printed in Translations and Reprints VI no. 5 (Philadelphia, 1900), pp. 12-14.

title: The capitulary for Saxony: the death clauses
passage_first_words: If any one of the race of the Saxons hereafter concealed among them shall have wished to hide himself unbaptized, and shall have scorned to come to baptism and shall have wished to remain a pagan, let him be punished by death.
where_found: daventre (Deventer, on the Saxon march); diusburg; traiectum; read out by a count's man (act:hear_law)
why: The law that stands behind the baptismal vow already in the chest. Clauses 4, 7, 8 and 9 (eating meat in Lent, burning the dead, hiding unbaptised, sacrifice) are what a Saxon or East Frisian crewman fears in 793. Softened in 797. Translations and Reprints VI no. 5, pp. 2-4.

title: Charlemagne to King Offa: merchants, pilgrims, black stones and cloaks (796)
passage_first_words: You have written to us also about merchants. We will and command that they have protection and patronage in our realm, lawfully, according to the ancient custom of trading.
where_found: lundenwic (the reeve's copy, from 796); quentovic and dorestad (the toll men are told of it); hamwic
why: The first trade letter between an English and a Frankish king, and it is about the player's own goods: querns ('black stones') going out, cloaks of the right length coming back, and traders who hide among pilgrims to dodge the toll. The earlier research thought no free English existed; Browne's lectures give it nearly whole. Checked against Gutenberg #71904.

title: Alcuin asks leave to fetch the books of York to Tours (796/797)
passage_first_words: But I, your poor servant, need some of the more abstruse books of scholastic learning which I had in my own land by the devoted labour of my master, and to some extent of myself.
where_found: eoforwic (the letter's errand ends there, from 797); namnetis (the Loire mouth: the way up to Tours); rotomagus
why: 'Send some of our young men to pick out what I need, and bring to France the flowers of Britain.' Books crossing the sea by ship in the game's first years: the plainest hook there is for a carrying chain from York to the Loire. Checked against Gutenberg #71904 (Browne's footnote marks left out).

title: Alcuin to Bishop Higbald and the monks of Lindisfarne (793)
passage_first_words: When I was with you, your friendly love was wont to give me much joy. And now that I am absent the calamity of your affliction greatly saddens me every day.
where_found: lindisfarena (from late summer 793); bebbanburg; eoforwic
why: The chest already has Alcuin's letter to King Aethelred in the game's own draft; this is the companion letter to the monks themselves, in a free translation that passes the rule. Browne gives long extracts of both, so the draft can be checked against him. Checked against Gutenberg #71904.

title: Alcuin's verses over the door of the writing room at Tours
passage_first_words: Here let the scribes sit who copy out the words of the Divine Law, and likewise the hallowed sayings of holy fathers. Let them beware of interspersing their own frivolities in the words they copy
where_found: any abbey or minster with a writing room, as a text read on the wall (act:read_text): parisius, mogontia, colonia, eoforwic, traiectum
why: How a book was made, in the makers' own rule: correct exemplars, points in their places, 'it is a noble work to write out holy books, nor shall the scribe fail of his due reward'. Short enough for one panel. Checked against the scan's text (Alcuin and the Rise of the Christian Schools, ch. on Tours).

title: Einhard: the king who kept writing tablets under his pillow (Life of Charles, 25)
passage_first_words: He tried also to learn to write, and for this purpose used to carry with him and keep under the pillow of his couch tablets and writing-sheets that he might in his spare moments accustom himself to the formation of letters.
where_found: from c. 830: noviomagus (the palace at Nijmegen), colonia, mogontia, parisius; before that the same thing is told as news of the king
why: Answers 'who could read': the greatest king in the west read Latin, understood Greek and never learned to form his letters. It makes the player's own unlettered skipper ordinary. Written c. 817-836. Printed 1905 (King's Classics; the brief cites the 1907 reprint). Checked against Gutenberg #48870.

title: Einhard: the old songs written down, the months and the twelve winds (Life of Charles, 29)
passage_first_words: He also wrote out the barbarous and ancient songs, in which the acts of the kings and their wars were sung, and committed them to memory. He also began a grammar of his native language.
where_found: from c. 830: noviomagus, colonia, mogontia, parisius
why: The only witness that the songs sung in halls were once put in a book (now lost), and a list of Frankish names for the months and the twelve winds that the game's calendar and wind rose can show. Checked against Gutenberg #48870.

title: Notker: the two Irishmen who cried wisdom for sale among the traders (Deeds of Charles I.1)
passage_first_words: Now it happened, when he had begun to reign alone in the western parts of the world, and the pursuit of learning had been almost forgotten throughout all his realm
where_found: told at quentovic, rotomagus or namnetis (the coast of Gaul, where the tale sets it) from the start, as a story heard; as a book from c. 885 at mogontia and up the Rhine (it was written at St Gall)
why: Scholars come over the sea 'along with certain traders of Britain' and set up at the market with nothing to sell: 'Ho, everyone that desires wisdom, let him draw near and take it at our hands; for it is wisdom that we have for sale.' It is the game's own claim (knowledge is the treasure) in a period joke. Checked against Gutenberg #48870.

title: Notker: Charles tells the Northmen's ships from merchants' by their build, and weeps (Deeds of Charles II.14)
passage_first_words: It happened too that on his wanderings Charles once came unexpectedly to a certain maritime city of Narbonensian Gaul. When he was dining quietly in the harbour of this town, it happened that some Norman scouts made a piratical raid.
where_found: as a book from c. 885: mogontia, colonia; as an old man's tale from c. 840 in any Frankish port
why: 'Some thought them Jews, some African or British merchants', but the king knew them 'by the build of the ships and their speed'. This is the lookout's skill the game already has, told as legend. Grant writes 'Norman' for Northman. Checked against Gutenberg #48870.

title: Notker: the Frisians and the little cloaks (Deeds of Charles I.34)
passage_first_words: But the habits of man change; and when the Franks, in their wars with the Gauls, saw the latter proudly wearing little striped cloaks, they dropped their national customs and began to imitate the Gauls.
where_found: dorestad and the Frisian ports as a standing joke from the start; as a book from c. 885 on the Rhine
why: The brief names it: Frisians selling short cloaks at the price of long ones, and the emperor's answer ('What is the good of those little napkins?'). It pairs with the cloak clause of the letter to Offa and with cloth as a trade good. Checked against Gutenberg #48870.

title: Rimbert: pirates take the merchants' ships and nearly forty books (Life of Anskar, 10)
passage_first_words: It may suffice for me to say that while they were in the midst of their journey they fell into the hands of pirates. The merchants with whom they were travelling, defended themselves vigorously and for a time successfully
where_found: birka (the voyage's end, from 830); sliesthorp (Hedeby, from the 850s, when it has a church); written c. 870, so as a book only after that, at sliesthorp or ripa
why: A missionary takes passage with merchants to Birka, the ship is taken and the books go to the raiders: the game's raid card told from the hold. It also means that somewhere in the Baltic a raider has forty Latin books he cannot read, which is a chain waiting to be written. Checked against the Fordham copy; ship from the 1921 scan.

title: Rimbert: Frideburg of Birka, her wine and her alms sent to Dorestad (Life of Anskar, 20)
passage_first_words: This devout woman, whose name was Frideburg, who was deserving of praise for the goodness of her life and the constancy of her faith, continued even to old age.
where_found: birka (c. 845-860); dorestad, where her daughter Catla brought the money and gave it to the poor and the churches
why: A rich Christian woman at Birka keeps bought wine by her for her last rites and tells her daughter to carry her wealth to Dorestad, 'There are there many churches, priests, and clergy, and a multitude of poor people'. It ties two of the game's ports by name and is a passenger job as it stands. Year approximate (?).

title: Rimbert: the Swedes cast lots before the walls in Courland (Life of Anskar, 30)
passage_first_words: As they were greatly disturbed and knew not what they should do, they resolved to enquire by casting lots whether their gods were willing to aid them either to obtain a victory or to get away from the place where they were.
where_found: birka (the merchants there told it to Anskar); grobin (Seeburg, the town the Swedes had taken first, is usually placed at Grobina (?))
why: Lots cast to learn which god will help, and it is merchants who advise trying the god of the Christians. The source for the act:ask_omen and for how two faiths sit side by side in a ship's company. Year approximate (?).

title: The Annals of Xanten: the years 845 to 850
passage_first_words: According to their custom the Northmen plundered Eastern and Western Frisia and burned the town of Dordrecht, with two other villages, before the eyes of Lothaire, who was then in the castle of Nimwegen, but could not punish the crime.
where_found: noviomagus (Nijmegen, where Lothar watched); colonia; daventre; from the year after each annal
why: The only free English of a Frankish annal that names the player's home town burning. Robinson writes 'Dordrecht' where the Latin has Dorestad: the game must put Dorestad in square brackets. Readings in European History vol. I, no. 70, pp. 158-161. The scan's text has double spaces and line-break hyphens; cleaned here.

title: The Chronicle: the first three ships of the Northmen (annal 787, for 789)
passage_first_words: This year King Bertric took Edburga the daughter of Offa to wife. And in his days came first three ships of the Northmen from the land of robbers.
where_found: hamwic (the reeve rode from Dorchester to Portland, a day west); lundenwic; as hearsay from the start, as a written annal from c. 892
why: The reeve took them for traders and 'would drive them to the king's town; for he knew not what they were; and there was he slain'. It is four years old when the game starts and it is about a toll man meeting ships. Checked against Gutenberg #657 (Ingram's text, Everyman 1912).

title: The Chronicle: three Irishmen in a boat without oars, and the hairy star (annal 891)
passage_first_words: And three Scots came to King Alfred in a boat without any oars from Ireland; whence they stole away, because they would live in a state of pilgrimage, for the love of God, they recked not where.
where_found: hamwic and the West Saxon ports from 892; duiblinn; a sea card off Cornwall in the summer of 891 could meet the boat itself
why: A boat 'made of two hides and a half', food for seven nights, landfall in Cornwall in seven nights: the smallest sea voyage on record, with the men's names. The comet in the same annal is one for the sky. Checked against Gutenberg #657.

title: The Chronicle: Alfred's long ships, neither Frisian nor Danish (annal 897, for 896)
passage_first_words: Then King Alfred gave orders for building long ships against the esks, which were full-nigh twice as long as the others. Some had sixty oars, some more
where_found: hamwic from 897; a shipyard site in Wessex; frisian ports, since the same annal names the Frisians who died in the king's ships
why: 'They were not shaped either after the Frisian or the Danish model': the one line in the sources that treats Frisian ship-building as a known pattern, and the annal goes on to name Frisian seamen (Wulfheard, Ebb and Ethelere, each called a Frieslander) killed fighting for Alfred. Good for the heirs' century. Checked against Gutenberg #657.

title: King Alfred's letter in front of the Pastoral Care (c. 890)
passage_first_words: So general was its decay in England that there were very few on this side of the Humber who could understand their rituals in English, or translate a letter from Latin into English; and I believe that there were not many beyond the Humber.
where_found: from c. 890 at every English bishop's seat, each copy with an aestel on it (Sweet: a clasp) worth fifty mancuses: lundenwic, hamwic (for Winchester), dofras and fordwic (for Canterbury), dommoc (?)
why: The fullest answer to 'who could read' in the whole period, and it says the churches 'stood filled with treasures and books' before everything was 'ravaged and burnt'. It also prices a book's furniture (50 mancuses is 1,500 pennies, three times the player's starting debt) and forbids anyone to take the book from the minster. Checked against the scan's text (EETS OS 45, pp. 2-8).

title: Asser: Alfred wins the book of Saxon poems (Life of Alfred, 23)
passage_first_words: Now on a certain day his mother was showing him and his brothers a book of Saxon poetry, which she held in her hand, and finally said: 'Whichever of you can soonest learn this volume, to him will I give it.'
where_found: hamwic and West Saxon minsters from c. 893; before that told of the king
why: A book of English verse owned by a lay woman in the 850s, wanted for its painted first letter, and won by learning it by heart from a reader, not by reading. It shows that 'to learn a book' meant to have it read to you: the game's crewman who reads part of Beowulf is the same custom. Checked against Gutenberg #63384.

title: Alfred and Guthrum's peace: trading across the line (clause 5)
passage_first_words: But if it happen, that from necessity any of them will have traffic with us, or we with them, with cattle and with goods, that is to be allowed in this wise; that hostages be given in pledge of peace
where_found: lundenwic from 886 (the border ran up the Thames and the Lea); gipeswic on the Danish side; read out at a folk-moot (act:hear_law)
why: The rule a merchant lives under between English and Danish England: no going over without leave, trade only with hostages given 'as evidence whereby it may be known that the party has a clean back'. It is ready-made card logic (a surety, or a risk). Date 878-890, usually put at 886 (?). Checked against the scan's text (Thorpe vol. I, p. 157).

title: Of people's ranks: the merchant who fared thrice over the wide sea
passage_first_words: And if a merchant thrived, so that he fared thrice over the wide sea by his own means, then was he thenceforth of thane-right worthy.
where_found: eoforwic (Archbishop Wulfstan's own book, c. 1002-1023 (?)); lundenwic; as a saying in English ports long before it was written
why: The one sentence in English law that makes sea trade a road to rank. It can be the house's long goal in the English ports: three crossings in the house's own ship, and a thane's standing. The text looks back to 'once' in English law, so the custom is older than the writing. Checked against the scan's text (Thorpe vol. I, Ranks, clause 6, pp. 192-193).

title: The laws of Ine: the stranger off the road, and the chapman up the country (20 and 25)
passage_first_words: If a far-coming man, or a stranger, journey through a wood out of the highway, and neither shout nor blow his horn, he is to be held for a thief, either to be slain or redeemed.
where_found: hamwic (West Saxon law; Alfred copied Ine's laws after his own, so they are in force through the game); lundenwic; sarre and fordwic have the Kentish twin (Wihtred 28)
why: What a foreign trader must do the moment he steps off the quay: keep to the road, make a noise, and buy 'before witnesses', or be taken for a thief. Each clause is one card. Checked against the scan's text (Thorpe vol. I, pp. 115-119); clause 25 follows as 'If a chapman traffic up among the people, let him do it before witnesses.'

title: The laws of Alfred: of chapmen and the men they take with them (34)
passage_first_words: It is also directed to chapmen, that they bring the men whom they take up with them before the king's reeve at the folk-mote, and let it be stated how many of them there are
where_found: hamwic and lundenwic from c. 890; the reeve at any West Saxon port says it (act:hear_law)
why: The skipper answers for his crew: he shows them to the reeve, counts them, and takes only men he can bring to justice later. This is the law behind 'hire' and 'pay_off' in an English port after 890. Checked against the scan's text (Thorpe vol. I, p. 83).

title: King Cnut's letter from Rome: the roads and tolls opened to traders (1027)
passage_first_words: Canute, king of all England, Denmark, Norway, and part of the Swedes, to Ethelnoth, metropolitan, and Elfric archbishop of York, and to all bishops, nobles, and to the whole nation of the English high and low, health.
where_found: lundenwic and eoforwic from 1027 (read out in the shire courts); hleidr or its successor Roskilde (?); colonia, on the road to Rome it speaks of
translator: John Sharpe (d. 1859 (?)), revised by J. A. Giles (d. 1884)
why: A king bargains with the emperor so that 'my subjects, traders, as well as those who went on a religious account, should peaceably go and return from Rome, without any molestation from warders of barriers, or tax-gatherers'. A real toll-free charter for the late game. Kept in William of Malmesbury (c. 1125), who dates it 1031; the journey was 1027. Checked against Gutenberg #50778. Sharpe's first printing was 1815.

title: The Frisian wife (Exeter Book, gnomic verses)
passage_first_words: Dear is the welcome guest to the Frisian wife, when the vessel stands, his ship is come, and her husband to home, her own provider, and she calls him in, washes his weedy garment, and to him gives new raiment
where_found: sung or said in any English port that sees Frisian ships (lundenwic, gipeswic, eoforwic, hamwic) from the start; best given at home, at dorestad or medemelacha, by the player's own household
why: Seven lines in an English book about the player's own people: the ship comes in, the wife washes the sea-stained clothes and gives new ones. The only home-coming scene of a North Sea trader from the period, and the natural words for the winter screen. Written down c. 970, older in the mouth. Checked against the scan's text (Codex Exoniensis p. 339).

title: The Whale, called Fastitocalon (Exeter Book)
passage_first_words: Now again I sing about the fishes' kind; I will in poetry, by words, make known, through the understanding, concerning the great Whale, which is unwillingly often met, cruel and fierce to seafarers
where_found: any English minster (act:read_text); or told by a crewman at sea on a calm day when whales are seen (a crew card)
why: Seafarers take the whale for an island, moor to it, light a fire and are drowned. A sea yarn with a sermon on the end, and the monks' own. It gives the chart's unknown waters something to be afraid of that the period really feared. Checked against the scan's text (Codex Exoniensis pp. 360-361).

title: Widsith, the far-wanderer
passage_first_words: Widsith spake, his word-hoard unlocked, who farthest had fared among folk of earth through tribes of men, oft taking in hall rich meed of gold.
where_found: from a singer in a hall (act:song) at bebbanburg, eoforwic or lundenwic; a Frisian singer such as Bernlef would know its matter
why: A singer's list of every people and king he has (he says) visited, Frisians, Danes, Swedes, Wends and Franks among them: the chart's peoples as a man of 793 would name them, and a ready hint system ('I was with the ...') for places still under fog. Date of making disputed (7th to 10th century (?)); written down c. 970. Checked against the scan's text (The Oldest English Epic, section Widsith; the page number is unreadable in the scan (?)).

title: The Lay of Hildebrand
passage_first_words: I heard it said that as foemen in fight sole faced each other Hildebrand and Hathubrand, two hosts between. There son and father their fighting-gear tested
where_found: mogontia (written on the blank outer leaves of a Fulda book c. 830, so from then); as a song much earlier in any Saxon, Frankish or Frisian hall
why: The only heroic song of the mainland Germans to survive, and it survives because two monks at Fulda filled a spare leaf with it: the perfect example of song turning into book by accident. A father must fight his son; the end is lost. Checked against the scan's text (The Oldest English Epic, pp. 173-177; the scan's 'f oemen' corrected).

title: The Battle of Brunanburh (Chronicle, 937)
passage_first_words: Athelstan King, Lord among Earls, Bracelet-bestower and Baron of Barons, He with his brother, Edmund Atheling, Gaining a lifelong Glory in battle
where_found: from 938 in English ports (legacaestir, eoforwic, lundenwic); duiblinn has the losers' side of it (Olaf Guthfrithson sailed home to Dublin)
why: The Chronicle breaks into verse for the year: the fleet of Dublin beaten and the Northmen going home 'over the deep water, Dublin to seek'. A news item that is also a poem, for the heirs' time. First words quoted from memory of Tennyson's Ballads and Other Poems (1880); the page could not be fetched: check (?). Ingram 1823 has a plainer version in Gutenberg #657.

title: The monk and his pet cat (Pangur Ban)
passage_first_words: I and my white Pangur Have each his special art: His mind is set on hunting mice, Mine is upon my special craft.
where_found: from an Irish scholar on his way to the Rhine: colonia, mogontia, a passenger out of duiblinn or hi; written in a monk's notebook near Lake Constance (the Reichenau Primer, now at St Paul in Carinthia)
why: The scholar's work told lightly: the cat hunts mice, the monk hunts meanings. It sits with 'Bitter is the wind tonight' (already in the chest, same translator, same kind of margin) and gives a learned passenger something to recite. Checked against Gutenberg #32030.

title: The scribe (A hedge of trees surrounds me)
passage_first_words: A hedge of trees surrounds me, A blackbird's lay sings to me; Above my lined booklet The trilling birds chant to me.
where_found: the same hands as the Viking quatrain already in the chest (the margins of the St Gall Priscian, written in Ireland c. 845 and carried to the Rhine): hi, duiblinn's churches, or an Irish passenger
why: A scribe writing out of doors in summer. Eight lines, a picture the user can draw, and the lightest possible note on how a book was made. Meyer's 'Colum Cille the Scribe' ('My hand is weary with writing') in the same book is a good second. Checked against Gutenberg #32030.

title: Hávamál: Othin wins the runes (stanzas 139-146)
passage_first_words: I ween that I hung on the windy tree, Hung there for nights full nine; With the spear I was wounded, and offered I was To Othin, myself to myself
where_found: from a rune carver or a skald (act:song) at sliesthorp, ripa, skiringssal, birka, uppsalir; as a rune stick in the chest (form rune_stick, like the Hávamál stanzas already there)
why: The chest has 27 stanzas of Hávamál's guest-wisdom and none of its rune part. These stanzas say where runes come from and ask the carver's questions ('Knowest how one shall write, knowest how one shall rede?'). Same translator and edition as the stanzas already in the file. Bellows's Sigrdrifumol 6-13 (winning-runes, wave-runes for ships) is a second pick. Checked against Gutenberg #73533.

title: Egil's Saga: the runes on the whalebone (ch. 75)
passage_first_words: Next he searched the bed in which she had lain, and there he found a piece of whalebone whereon were runes. Egil read them, then cut the runes and scraped them off into the fire.
where_found: told in Norway and its neighbours from c. 950 (the journey to Vermland): skiringssal, ogvaldsnes; a card where a sick person's kin ask a rune-wise crewman for help
why: 'Runes none should grave ever Who knows not to read them.' A neighbour's son cut love-runes wrongly and made a girl ill; Egil reads, scrapes and burns them and cuts new ones. It shows runes on a bit of bone as an everyday object that can be read, and misread. The saga was written c. 1230 (toldLater). Checked against sagadb's text of Green 1893.

title: Saxo: Amleth changes the letter cut on wood (Danish History, book III)
passage_first_words: Two retainers of Feng then accompanied him, bearing a letter graven on wood--a kind of writing material frequent in old times; this letter enjoined the king of the Britons to put to death the youth who was sent over to him.
where_found: told at hleidr (Lejre, the old Danish kings' seat) and sliesthorp as an old story of the Danes from the start; never as a book in the game's years
why: A rune stick as a sealed letter carried over the North Sea, read on the way by the man it condemns, shaved clean and cut again. It tells the player what a rune stick is for and why a carrier should know his runes. Saxo wrote c. 1200 from old Danish lays (toldLater). Checked against Gutenberg #1150.
